public.e: The adjective and noun are derived from Late Middle English publik, publike (“(adjective) generally observable, public; relating to the general public or public affairs; (noun) a generally observable place or situation”).
public.g: Able to be known or seen by everyone; happening without concealment; open to general view.

public.e: Semantic loan from Russian па́блик (páblik) and Ukrainian па́блік (páblik, “public webpage on a blog or on social media”), both borrowed from English public: see etymology 1.

publican.e: Probably from public house (“(Britain) bar or tavern, often also selling food and sometimes lodging, pub”) or public (“open to all members of a community”) + -an (suffix forming agent nouns), apparently originally used humorously.
publican.g: The landlord (manager or owner) of a public house (“a bar or tavern, often also selling food and sometimes lodging; a pub”).

publican.e: From Middle English publican, from Anglo-Norman publican, pupplican, Middle French publicain, and Old French publican, publicain, pupplican (“tax collector”) (modern French publicain), and from their etymon Latin pūblicānus (“tax collector”).
publican.g: A tax collector, especially one working in Judea and Galilee during New Testament times (1st century C.E.) who was generally regarded as sin

publish.e: From Middle English publicen (by analogy with banish, finish), from Old French publier, from Latin publicare (“to make public, show or tell to the people, make known, declare, also (and earlier) confiscate for public use”), from publicus (“pertaining to the people, public”); see public.
publish.g: To issue (something, such as printed work) for distribution and/or sale.

puff.e: From Middle English puff, puf, from Old English pyf (“a blast of wind, puff”), from Proto-West Germanic *puf(f)- (“to blow, puff”), of imitative origin.
puff.g: A sharp exhalation of a small amount of breath through the mouth.

puff.e: From Middle English puffen, from Old English pyffan (“to breathe out, blow with the mouth”).
puff.g: To emit smoke, gas, etc., in puffs.

pull.e: Verb from Middle English pullen, from Old English pullian (“to pull, draw, tug, pluck off”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Noun from Middle English pul, pull, pulle, from the verb pullen (“to pull”).
pull.g: To apply a force to (an object) so that it comes toward the person or thing applying the force.

pulling.e: From Middle English *pullynge, equivalent to pull + -ing.

pulpit.e: From Middle English pulpit, from Old French pulpite and Latin pulpitum (“platform”). Piecewise doublet of polypod.
pulpit.g: A raised platform in a church, sometimes enclosed, where the minister or preacher stands when giving the sermon; also, the lectern on such a

pulse.e: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pous, pouse (“regular beat of arteries, pulse; heartbeat; place on the body where a pulse is detectable; beat (of a musical instrument); energy, vitality”), from Anglo-Norman puls, pous, pus, and Middle French pouls, poulz, pous, Old French pous, pulz (“regular beat of arteries.
pulse.g: A normally regular beat felt when arteries near the skin (for example, at the neck or wrist) are depressed, caused by the heart pumping bloo

pulse.e: From Late Middle English pulse, Middle English pulsen (“to pulse, throb”), from Latin pulsāre, the present active infinitive of pulsō (“to push; to beat, batter, hammer, strike; to knock on; (figuratively) to drive or urge on, impel; to move; to agitate, disquiet, disturb”), the frequentative of pellō (“to drive, impel, propel, push.
pulse.g: To emit or impel (something) in pulses or waves.

punish.e: From Middle English punischen, from Anglo-Norman, Old French puniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of punir, from Latin puniō (“to inflict punishment upon”), from poena (“punishment, penalty”); see pain.
punish.g: To cause (a child, student, or someone else being looked after, or a suspect or criminal) to suffer for crime or misconduct, to administer d

punishment.e: From Middle English punishement, from Old French punissement, from punir (“to punish”). Equivalent to punish + -ment.
punishment.g: The act (action) or process of punishing, imposing and/or applying a sanction, typically by an authority or a person in authority (for examp

pupil.e: From Middle English pupille, from Anglo-Norman pupille (“orphan”), from Latin pūpillus (“orphan, minor”), variant of pūpulus (“little boy”), from pūpus (“child, boy”).
pupil.g: A learner at a school under the supervision of a teacher.

pupil.e: From Middle English pupille, from Old French pupille, from Latin pūpilla (“pupil; little girl, doll”), named because of the small reflected image seen when looking into someone's eye.
pupil.g: The hole in the middle of the iris of the eye, through which light passes to be focused on the retina.

purchase.e: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”).
purchase.g: The acquisition of title to, or property in, anything for a price; buying for money or its equivalent.

pure.e: From Middle English pure, pur, from Old French pur, from Latin pūrus (“clean, free from dirt or filth, unmixed, plain”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“to cleanse, purify”).
pure.g: Free of flaws or imperfections; unsullied.

purely.e: From Middle English purely, equivalent to pure + -ly.

purge.e: From Middle English purgen, from Old French purgier, from Latin pūrgō (“to make pure, to cleanse”), from pūrus (“clean, pure”) + agō (“to make, to do”). The slang sense derived via the 2013 film The Purge.
purge.g: To clean thoroughly; to rid of impurities; to cleanse; to clear of (something unwanted).

purging.e: From Middle English purgynge; equivalent to purge + -ing.
purging.g: The act or an instance of eliminating contamination: a purification, a cleansing

purification.e: From Old French purificacion, from Latin pūrificātiō.
purification.g: The act or process of purifying; the removal of impurities.

purify.e: From Middle English purifien, purifyen, from Old French purifier, purifiier, from Latin pūrificō, pūrificāre, from pūrus (“pure; clean”).
purify.g: To cleanse, or rid of impurities.

purity.e: From pure + -ity, from Old French purete, from Latin puritas.
purity.g: The state or degree of being pure.

purloin.e: From Middle English purloynen (“to remove”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman purloigner (“to put far away”), one of the variants of Old French porloignier.
purloin.g: To take the property of another, often in breach of trust; to appropriate wrongfully; to steal.

purple.e: From Middle English purple, purpel, from Old English purpul (“purple”, adjective), taken from Old English purpure (“purple colour”, noun), from Latin purpura (“purple dye, shellfish”), from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple-fish”), perhaps of Semitic origin. The sense of "imperial power" is from the wearing of the color purple by emperors and kings.
purple.g: A colour between red and blue; violet, though often closer to magenta.

purpose.e: From Middle English purpos, from Old French purposer (“to propose”) (with conjugation altered based on poser), from Latin prō- (“forth”) + pōnere (“place, put”), hence Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere. By surface analysis, pur- + pose (“halt, pause, put, place”).
purpose.g: The end for which something is done, is made or exists.

purpose.e: From Middle English purposen, from Old French purposer (“to propose”).
purpose.g: To have or set as one's purpose or aim; resolve to accomplish; intend; plan.

purse.e: From Middle English purs, from Old English purs (“purse”), partly from pusa (“wallet, bag, scrip”) and partly from burse (“pouch, bag”). Old English pusa comes from Proto-West Germanic *pusō.
purse.g: A small bag for carrying money.

pursue.e: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor).
pursue.g: To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase.

pursuit.e: From Middle English pursuyte, from Old French poursuite, from the verb porsuir (“to pursue”).

push.e: From Middle English pushen, poshen, posson, borrowed from Middle French pousser (Modern French pousser) from Old French poulser, from Latin pulsare (“to beat, strike”), frequentative of pellere (past participle pulsus). Partly displaced native Old English sċūfan, whence Modern English shove.
push.g: To apply a force to (an object) such that it moves away from the person or thing applying the force.

put.e: From Middle English putten, pitten, pytten, puten, poten, from Old English putian, *pūtian ("to push, put out"; attested by derivative putung (“pushing, impulse, instigation, urging”)) and potian (“to push, thrust, strike, butt, goad”), both from Proto-West Germanic *putōn, from Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to stick, stab”), which is of uncertain origin.
put.g: To physically place (something or somebody, in, at, around, etc. someplace)

put.e: Unknown. Perhaps related to Welsh pwt, itself possibly borrowed from English butt (“stub, thicker end”).
put.g: A fellow, especially an eccentric or elderly one; a duffer.

putting.g: The action of the verb to putt.

puzzle.e: The verb, of uncertain origin, is attested first. Apparently cognate with Scots pousle, pouzle, poozle (“to trifle; poke or potter around aimlessly; search about with uncertainty”), Saterland Frisian puzelje (“to work hard and continuously”), West Frisian peuzelje (“to trifle, work slowly.
